newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia shares end up, boosted by Petrol.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia shares end up, boosted by Petrol.

text.p: Slovenian shares ended 0.24 percent higher on Tuesday, boosted, traders said, by a 2.28 percent rise of petrol trader Petrol, which made its debut on the Ljubljana bourse on Monday.

"Petrol is one of the largest Slovenian companies with good business results and solid plans for the future therefore its price is expected to rise to about 18,000 tolars in the next two weeks," one said.
Analysts said shares could firm by one percent by the end of the week on expectations of fresh foreign investment later this month.

"As soon as foreigners return, the index will probably jump by up to 10 percent in a period of a single day. The question remains whether they will be back in May," said Goran Brankovic, a trader of bank Nova Ljubljanska Banka.

The Bank of Slovenia in February blocked foreign buying, saying international investors must open custodian accounts at Slovenian banks in order to trade in securities. Since then the blue-chip index has dropped by 20.8 percent, while average daily volume has fallen to a tenth of its previous value.
Banks said first custodian accounts were expected to be opened in the middle of May.
"Fresh foreign investment could push the index up by 30 to 50 percent in a matter of two months," Brankovic said.
The SBI index rose 3.18 points to 1,310.80.
Petrol was the most actively traded stock, closing at 17,530 tolars on volume of 1,467 shares for total turnover of 25.4 million tolars.
Overall 16 shares rose, one was unchanged, four fell and seven were untraded.
Bank UBK was the top gainer, climbing 5.26 percent to 6,000 tolars on volume of 109 shares.
Traders said UBK could grow further on speculation that foreign investors might be interested in shares of successful Slovenian banks, which are relatively cheap compared to similar banks abroad.

Preferred shares of bank Hipotekarna Banka Brezice led the decliners, falling 9.97 percent. Traders attributed the fall to the fact that investors were wary of small banks following the bankruptcy of Komercialna Banka Triglav in July 1996. -- Marja Novak, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
